analysis.one_liner: Puts a 10-cent refund on beer and soda containers nationwide to cut litter and pay for state recycling.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never received a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required a 10-cent refund value on every beer, soda, mineral water, and wine cooler container sold nationwide, with a system to collect deposits at sale and pay them back when containers are returned. Unclaimed deposits would go to states for pollution prevention and recycling programs. Distributors and retailers would have to handle returns, and metal cans with detachable pull-tabs would be banned. States already achieving 70 percent recycling or reuse of beverage containers would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who return containers get their 10-cent deposit back, and anyone picking up litter — including scavengers, community groups, and cleanup crews — can redeem containers for cash. Local governments gain twice: less litter and landfill waste, plus unclaimed deposits routed to state recycling and pollution prevention programs [S2][S3]. The bill's findings argue that state deposit laws have proven inexpensive to administer and shift recycling and litter-control costs onto beverage producers and consumers rather than communities [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every beer, soda, mineral water, and wine cooler container would carry a 10-cent refund value, paid back to anyone who returns the empty container to a retailer or distributor that sells that brand [S2][S3].
Distributors would pay states the unclaimed deposits each year, and states could use that money for pollution prevention and recycling programs [S2][S3].
Retailers and distributors would be barred from dumping deposit containers or their metal, glass, or plastic in landfills, and metal cans with detachable pull-tab openings would be banned [S2][S3].
States that demonstrate a 70 percent or better recycling or reuse rate for beverage containers would be exempt from the national requirements, preserving stronger state programs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beverage distributors and retailers would collect and administer deposits and pay a handling fee of at least 2 cents per returned container; those costs would likely show up partly in beverage prices. Consumers pay the deposit up front but get it back when they return the container. Beverage and container makers would face the refund system, the pull-tab ban, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation for most rules [S3].

drawbacks.text: Consumers pay the deposit up front; anyone who never bothers to return containers forfeits the money, which then flows to the state rather than back to them [S3].

Retailers and distributors must handle returned containers and pay at least 2 cents per container in handling costs, and retailers must take back any brand and container type they have sold in the past three months — a real storage and logistics burden that the industry argued raises prices [S3].
The deposit does not apply to noncarbonated drinks like juice, water, or sports drinks, so the system covers only part of the beverage stream [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main costs fall on the beverage industry and retailers in the form of deposit administration and handling, and most of that cost is recoverable or passed on in small amounts; the main benefits — less litter, lower landfill and cleanup costs, and dedicated state recycling funding — go to the public. The bill itself cites state deposit laws as inexpensive to administer and effective, which is the strongest evidence on its side [S3]. The main honest criticism is the upfront deposit on consumers and the handling burden placed on small retailers.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hatfield introduced the bill on March 11, 1992, with bipartisan cosponsors — 2 Republicans and 6 Democrats joined him [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S5].
The bill expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993, without the committee ever reporting it to the Senate [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beverage producers, distributors, retailers, and container manufacturers avoided a nationwide deposit system, the pull-tab ban, and landfill disposal prohibitions; communities got no new recycling funding or litter reduction.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: a Republican senator from Oregon introduced it with cosponsors split 2 Republicans and 6 Democrats, but no vote was ever taken to test broader support [S4].

industries.note: They would have to collect deposits on every container sold, pay states unclaimed refunds, and face civil penalties for noncompliance. Their gain from the bill dying was avoiding a nationwide deposit system; the public cost is continued litter and landfill waste.

Retailers would have to charge the deposit, take back empties for any brand sold in the prior three months, and store returned containers. They often pass these handling costs to customers, but deposit laws shift cleanup costs off taxpayers and communities.

The bill bans metal cans with detachable pull-tab openings and bars disposing of covered container material in landfills, raising packaging design and disposal costs. High return rates would, however, feed recyclable material back into manufacturing.

industries.industry: Recycling industry and state recycling programs
industries.note: Unclaimed deposits would fund state pollution prevention and recycling programs, and redeemed containers would supply clean, sorted recyclable material.
